title: Living in a closed-up house
summary: Close windows, doors and anything that pulls in outside air, but don’t seal the house airtight: fallout shelter doesn’t need it, and people need air. Never burn anything in a sealed room. Keep warm without flame first; burn only if the cold itself becomes a danger to life, and then under every carbon monoxide rule.
doFirst: Close and lock windows and doors. Turn off fans, air conditioners and forced-air heating units that bring in air from outside (CDC).
Never burn anything in a sealed room. Closing up the house is not sealing it airtight: structures do not need to be airtight to protect against fallout radiation (FEMA planning guidance).
Never heat the house with an oven or gas range, and never run a generator, grill, camp stove, charcoal or a fuel lantern indoors (CDC). See Carbon monoxide.
Cold? Warm people without flame first: one small room, layers, blankets, sleeping bags and each other. See Stay warm when the heat is out.
Keep battery CO alarms near where people sleep (CDC, CPSC). If one sounds, get everyone outside now (CPSC). See Carbon monoxide.

list: Close and lock all windows and doors (CDC).

Turn off fans, air conditioners and forced-air heating units that bring in air from outside, if you can (CDC, Ready.gov). In houses and apartments, that includes window fans and any heating or cooling system that brings in outside air (New York City, Response Guide: Radiological and Nuclear Emergencies).

Close fireplace dampers (CDC, Ready.gov), but only when no fire is burning. Open the damper before you light a fire, and never close it until the fire is out and the embers are cold (Massachusetts Department of Fire Services). See Wood stoves and fireplaces.
Bring pets inside (CDC, Ready.gov). Bring in and wipe off any supplies from outside that your pets will need for at least 24 hours (CDC).

blocks.warn: Never burn anything in a sealed room. A closed-up house still needs air, and anything that burns fuel makes carbon monoxide.

blocks.p: Closing up the house means shutting out the outside air that fans and open windows pull in. It does not mean sealing the house: structures do not need to be airtight to protect against fallout radiation, and FEMA’s planning guidance says to keep enough ventilation for the air indoors to stay fit to breathe. Don’t tape or cover doors, windows or vents to make the house airtight (this app’s reading of FEMA).

list: Never heat the house with an oven or gas range, and never run a generator, grill, camp stove, charcoal or a fuel lantern indoors (CDC). See Carbon monoxide.
Even with doors and windows open, a closed or partly closed space can trap carbon monoxide and let it build to deadly levels quickly (CPSC; Carbon monoxide).
Older civil defence handbooks (Office of Civil Defense, 1968; FEMA, 1985) allow a stove indoors with ventilation, and the 1985 handbook names a camp stove. This app doesn’t: it follows CDC and CPSC.

blocks.p: A CO alarm still means what Carbon monoxide says, even during a fallout warning: “If one sounds, get everyone outside now (CPSC).” Going out means going into fallout, which is one more reason nothing burns in a closed-up house.

blocks.label: Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors

blocks.p: This app’s rule for a closed-up house in winter: warmth without flame comes first, for the whole sheltering period. If the cold itself becomes a danger to life, run the stove or heater under the carbon monoxide rules in full, accepting that outside air comes in. Nothing ever burns in a sealed room.

A furnace or boiler vented to the outside that still has power to run is the house’s normal heat, not a stove or heater added for the emergency (this app’s reading). Turn off any forced-air heating that brings in air from outside (CDC), and keep its outside vents clear (What a furnace needs, in Stay warm when the heat is out). The rule above is for when it can’t run.
Warmth without flame, as in Stay warm when the heat is out:

list: Pick one small room on the sheltered side of the house, with few windows, and live in that. Close off the rest (University of Missouri Extension, CDC; Stay warm when the heat is out).
Put on layers, a hat and socks, and use blankets and sleeping bags (FEMA, National Institute on Aging; Stay warm when the heat is out).

Bed is the warmest place, with other family members and lots of covers (University of Missouri Extension; Stay warm when the heat is out). Babies sleep differently: see Stay warm when the heat is out.

blocks.warn: Babies under 1 year must never sleep in a cold room (CDC). Check older people often: they make less body heat (CDC). They are among those most at risk from the cold (Stay warm when the heat is out).

blocks.p: No source opened gives an indoor temperature at which the cold becomes a danger to life (Stay warm when the heat is out lists the figures sources do give). Watch babies and older people first, and use the Hypothermia protocol for the signs.
If the cold becomes a danger to life, these are the only ways to burn anything, each under every rule in its own topic:

list: A wood stove or fireplace vented to the outside, with the damper open, by every rule in Wood stoves and fireplaces, including putting the fire out before anyone sleeps.

A kerosene or propane heater made for indoor use, only under every condition in Kerosene and propane heaters. Those conditions include a door open to the rest of the house and an outside window open about 1 inch (2.5 cm): that is the outside air this rule accepts.
Working CO alarms in the house, whatever you burn (Carbon monoxide).

blocks.p: Stay warm when the heat is out says to go somewhere with heat if you can’t keep the house warm. During a fallout warning that means going outside: read How long to stay in first.

blocks.label: Stay warm when the heat is out

blocks.p: Use flashlights or battery lanterns, not candles or fuel lanterns (CDC, CPSC; Carbon monoxide).

list: An unvented fuel-burning heater: “Turn it off when you go to sleep or leave the room, and never run it where anyone is sleeping (CPSC, US Fire Administration; Carbon monoxide protocol).”
A wood stove or fireplace: “Put the fire out before you go to sleep or leave the house (US Fire Administration, FEMA).”
For keeping warm at night without a flame, see Sleep warm.

blocks.p: Food and drinks that are sealed or were already inside can be used (CDC). Use the water stored in the house and the toilet arrangements in these topics, so nobody has to go outside for them.

blocks.label: Toilets when the water is off

sections.h: When someone has to go out

list: Keep it short: see How long to stay in.
Coming back, carefully take off the outer layer of clothes before coming inside (CDC), so radioactive dust doesn’t shake loose (Ready.gov). Put them in a bag (Ready.gov).
Wash or wipe the skin and hair that were uncovered (Ready.gov).
Wipe off anything brought in from outside, such as pet supplies (CDC).

blocks.p: Officials will tell you if the house itself needs cleaning (CDC).
